topic:
Navigating a New City Alone  
Useful expressions: "ask for directions," "use a map app."
script: Hey everyone, welcome to "Chillwave B2".
I'm Ethan.
Tonight, let’s chat about figuring out a new city when you’re all by yourself.
I remember the first time I got lost in Seattle and had to ask for directions—turns out the guy I asked was on his way to the same place.
So, grab a snack, get comfy, and let’s make sense of maps and street signs together for a bit.
A few months ago, I moved to Seattle and got lost trying to find my apartment on the first day.
I was standing outside this tiny coffee shop near the train station, totally clueless.
Heh, I asked the barista for directions, but she just smiled and said, "You’re in the right place!"
Eventually, I pulled out my phone and used the map app to figure out which street I was actually on.
Turns out I’d walked past the apartment building three times before realizing it.
So, has anyone else ever had that moment where you’re sure you’re lost but you’re just missing something obvious?
A couple of weeks later, I decided to explore Pike Place Market without my phone.
I thought I had a good sense of direction, but the alleys there are like a maze.
A tourist stopped me and asked if I needed help—turns out I was two blocks away from where I thought I was.
I laughed it off and used the map app later to see how I’d gotten so turned around.
Sometimes, even when you think you’re keeping track, the city plays tricks on you.
Have you ever trusted your instincts too much and ended up somewhere unexpected?
Cities have a way of teaching you patience, don’t they?
Maps and strangers can both point you in the right direction—sometimes literally.
Heh, I still get lost in my own neighborhood sometimes, to be honest.
But there’s something kind of fun about stumbling into places you weren’t looking for.
Maybe you’ll find your favorite coffee shop or a park you never knew existed.
If you’ve got a story about getting lost—or found—drop us a line later, yeah?
"Hey, speaking of getting turned around—did you know saying 'I think I took a wrong turn' is a super polite way to hint you’re lost?"
"It’s like telling someone you’re not totally clueless but just need a little help steering back on track."
"For example: 'Excuse me, I think I took a wrong turn—could you tell me how to get to the library?' sounds way friendlier than 'I’m lost.' "
"Also, if you hit a dead end, that means you’re in a street with no way out, like a wall of buildings instead of a road."
"Next time you’re wandering, just say 'Oh no, this looks like a dead end' and someone might just save your night."
Navigating a new city’s like a game where the map’s optional—sometimes the best parts are the surprises.
Thanks for hanging out and sharing the journey, even the confusing bits.
Heh, maybe we’ll all get lost in a good way someday.
Night, everyone—drive safe, or walk slow, and keep exploring.
